get.description: List every REGISTERED activity type with its current pause state (issue #807). The list is driven by the registered activity catalogue, not the pause table, so a healthy activity appears with `paused: false` -- the read is a fleet inventory an operator scans during an incident, and one that only listed the already-broken things could not answer "is charge_card held?". An activity that is paused but NOT registered in this process is still listed, flagged `registered: false`, so a mistyped hold can never become invisible on the one surface used to find it. Cross-shard: an unreachable shard is named in `unavailable_shards` and drops `status` to "partial" rather than failing the read. Admin only.

200.description: Each entry carries activity_name, registered, queue_name, is_local, paused, paused_at, paused_reason, paused_actor, scope_shard_id, held_task_count (summed across shards), provenance_uniform, effective_scope, and a shards array of per-shard objects {shard_id, reason, paused_by, paused_at, scope_shard_id, held_task_count}. For an unpaused activity, paused is false and paused_at/paused_reason/paused_actor/scope_shard_id/effective_scope are null, held_task_count is 0 and shards is empty. queue_name and is_local are null for a paused-but-unregistered activity (this process has no catalogue entry to read them from); is_local matters because a local activity runs inline on the workflow worker and never takes a task-queue row, so a hold on one holds nothing. The top-level paused_reason/paused_actor/paused_at/scope_shard_id summarise the EARLIEST hold (tie-broken by shard id -- the same rule the pause mutation response uses, so the two surfaces never disagree). Because pause is idempotent and preserves the original provenance on a re-pause, a request landing over a pre-existing hold can leave shards disagreeing; provenance_uniform is false in that case and the shards array carries each shard's own story. Uniformity compares reason/paused_by/scope_shard_id and deliberately not paused_at, since each shard stamps its own NOW(). effective_scope ("fleet" | "partial_fleet" | "shard") reports what the hold ACTUALLY covers, derived from the shards that hold the activity versus the expected shard set (every pool plus every shard the router knows about) -- distinct from scope_shard_id, which records only the INTENT of the request that wrote each row. A fleet-wide pause that reached only some shards persists scope_shard_id = NULL on the shards it reached and no row at all on the ones it missed, so intent alone cannot distinguish it from a complete hold while the missed shards keep dispatching the activity; effective_scope is "partial_fleet" in that case (re-issue the pause). An unreachable shard counts as expected-but-not-holding -- the safe direction, since it may still be dispatching -- so a partial read also reports "partial_fleet". IMPORTANT: on a partial read, `paused: false` means only "not paused on the shards that could be reached" -- always check `status` before trusting a negative.

get.description: Get one activity type's pause state (issue #807). Returns 404 when the name is neither registered in this process NOR currently paused anywhere the read could reach. The pause arm of that rule is deliberate: an activity that is actively holding work is a real thing an operator must be able to inspect and then resume, so 404-ing it merely because this process does not have its handler registered would be a lie told during exactly the incident the endpoint exists for. Admin only.

parameters.description: The activity type to inspect, matched EXACTLY (no trimming) against both the registered catalogue and the pause table.
parameters.name: activity_name

200.description: `activity` is a single entry with the same shape as one element of `GET /activities` (see its notes). `status`/`unavailable_shards` are reported here too, and for the same reason: on a partial read `paused: false` means only "not paused on the shards that could be reached". A 404 is only returned when EVERY expected shard was inspected: the routes deliberately accept unregistered names, so "not in this process's catalogue and no pause row on the shards that answered" is reachable with a live hold sitting on a shard that did not answer, and asserting nonexistence there would deny a hold that is actively holding work. While any shard is unaccounted for the read fails closed with 503 naming those shards -- the same rule the (workflow_name, workflow_id) resolver applies.

404.description: The activity is neither registered in this process nor currently paused, AND every expected shard was inspected. A miss on an incomplete read is reported as 503 instead, so a 404 always means a fully-observed absence.

503.description: Harvest storage pool is not configured, OR the activity was not found while at least one expected shard could not be inspected -- the read fails closed rather than returning a 404 that could deny a live hold on the unreachable shard. The message names the shard(s) to re-check.

post.description: Hold dispatch for ONE activity type, fleet-wide, during a scoped downstream outage (issue #807). This is the surgical sibling of the queue pause (issue #619): use it when many activity types share a queue and holding the whole queue would also stop healthy work. While paused, no worker claims NEW tasks of that activity type; held tasks stay PENDING and are never failed, retried, or dead-lettered, and an already-RUNNING attempt finishes naturally. The relative `schedule_to_start` timer is suspended for held tasks; the absolute `schedule_to_close` deadline (issue #378) keeps ticking, so a long hold can still time out work carrying one -- a pause is not an SLA extension. The hold is applied on EVERY shard: it is fleet-wide by construction and there is no shard-scoped variant on this route. Idempotent: re-pausing an already-paused type is a 200 no-op that preserves the original reason and operator (`newly_paused: false`). Body and both of its fields are optional -- during an incident, containment must not wait on paperwork. A partially-applied hold is reported as 207, not 200 -- see the success-response notes. Admin only; audited as `activity.pause`, including rejected attempts. A pause is REFUSED with a 400 when the named activity is registered on this node as a LOCAL activity (`#[activity(local = true)]`): a local activity runs inline on the workflow worker and never takes a task-queue row, so the claim-path gate cannot hold it -- reporting a successful hold there would be a false green at exactly the moment an operator relies on it. Contain a local activity by pausing the queue its calling workflows dispatch on (issue #619), or via its circuit breaker if one is declared (issue #369).

parameters.description: The activity type to hold, matched EXACTLY. Leading or trailing whitespace is rejected with a 400 rather than trimmed: the hold is matched on exact equality, so a stray space would either hold nothing or hold a different activity while reporting success. Registration is NOT required -- a management process need not register every activity the fleet runs, so an unregistered name is accepted and surfaces on the read endpoints with `registered: false`. A registered name whose activity is LOCAL is rejected with a 400 (see the route description); an unregistered name is still accepted, since it may be a genuinely remote activity this node does not register.
parameters.name: activity_name

actor.description: Operator identity to record as `paused_by`. This is a LABEL, not authentication: it lets an automation attribute a hold to the human it acted for. The audit row always carries the AUTHENTICATED actor derived from the request headers and records the on-behalf-of relationship when the two differ, so this field can never rewrite the security trail. Defaults to the authenticated actor.

reason.description: Human-readable reason for the hold, surfaced on the read API and carried into the audit trail (the pause row is deleted on resume, so the audit row is the reason's only permanent home). Truncated to 500 characters. Defaults to "operator pause (no reason given)".

200.description: A hold applied to only SOME shards returns 207 Multi-Status with `ok: false` and `status: "partial"`, plus a `partial_failures` string naming the shards that were not reached (including a shard the router knows about but this process has no pool for). The hold is NOT in effect fleet-wide in that case -- the missed shards keep dispatching -- so re-issue the request (it is idempotent). A fully applied request returns 200 with `ok: true` and `status: "complete"`, and omits `partial_failures`. Cross-shard provenance: `held_task_count` is the fleet-wide sum, while the top-level `reason`/`paused_by`/`paused_at`/`scope_shard_id` describe the EARLIEST hold (tie-broken by shard id -- the same rule the read endpoints use). Because an idempotent re-pause preserves each shard's ORIGINAL provenance, a request landing over a pre-existing hold leaves the shards disagreeing: `shards` then carries every shard's own `{shard_id, newly_paused, reason, paused_by, paused_at, scope_shard_id, held_task_count}` and `provenance_uniform` is false. `provenance_uniform` compares `(reason, paused_by, scope_shard_id)` and deliberately NOT `paused_at`, since each shard stamps its own NOW(). `scope_shard_id` is always null for a hold placed by this route (fleet-wide); it is reported because the underlying column records the INTENT of whichever surface wrote each row.

partial_failures.description: Summary of the shards the hold could not be applied to. Present only on this status.

207.description: The hold reached only SOME shards. The body is the 200 body plus partial_failures naming the shards that did not apply it, so an operator can see the hold is not fleet-wide.

400.description: Blank, whitespace-padded, or oversized activity name; or a malformed request body (unknown fields are rejected, so a typo cannot become a silently-ignored setting).

500.description: Every shard failed; no hold is in effect.

503.description: Harvest storage pool is not configured.

post.summary: Hold dispatch for ONE activity type, fleet-wide, during a scoped downstream outage (issue #807).
post.x-harvest-idempotency: Re-pausing an already-paused activity returns 200 with `newly_paused: false` and preserves the original reason, operator, `paused_at` AND `scope_shard_id`. The response always describes the hold that is actually in effect, never the request.

post.description: Release a per-activity-type hold, fleet-wide (issue #807). Held tasks become immediately claimable again, and the time each task spent held is credited back to its `scheduled_at` so the thaw does not retroactively schedule-to-start-time-out the whole backlog. `released_reason`/`released_paused_by` echo the provenance of the hold that was released -- the pause row is deleted by the resume, so this is the last moment the *why* is recoverable. Body is optional and carries no fields; a bare POST resumes fleet-wide. Idempotent: resuming an activity that is not paused is a 200 no-op (`newly_resumed: false`). A partially-applied resume is reported as 207, not 200. Admin only; audited as `activity.resume`, including rejected attempts.

parameters.description: The activity type to release, matched EXACTLY. Leading or trailing whitespace is rejected with a 400 rather than trimmed, symmetrically with the pause route -- see its description for why.
parameters.name: activity_name

200.description: A resume applied to only SOME shards returns 207 Multi-Status with `ok: false`, `status: "partial"` and a `partial_failures` string. Work remains held on the shards that were not reached -- the safe direction, but not a completed thaw -- so re-issue the request (it is idempotent). A fully applied request returns 200 with `ok: true` and `status: "complete"`. Cross-shard provenance: the resume DELETES the pause rows, so this response and the audit row are the ONLY surviving record of what was released. `released_task_count` is the fleet-wide sum and `paused_duration_secs` the longest hold; the top-level `released_reason`/`released_paused_by` describe THAT same longest-held shard (tie-broken by lowest shard id), so the duration and the story it is paired with always come from one shard. `shards` carries every shard's own `{shard_id, newly_resumed, released_task_count, paused_duration_secs, released_reason, released_paused_by}`, and `provenance_uniform` is false when the released shards disagree on `(released_reason, released_paused_by)`. A shard that was not paused contributes null provenance and is ignored by the summary.

partial_failures.description: Summary of the shards the hold could not be applied to. Present only on this status.

207.description: The hold reached only SOME shards. The body is the 200 body plus partial_failures naming the shards that did not apply it, so an operator can see the hold is not fleet-wide.

400.description: Blank, whitespace-padded, or oversized activity name; or a request body that is not empty or `{}` (the route accepts no fields, so anything else is a typo).

500.description: Every shard failed; the hold may still be in effect.

503.description: Harvest storage pool is not configured.

post.summary: Release a per-activity-type hold, fleet-wide (issue #807).
post.x-harvest-idempotency: Resuming an activity that is not paused returns 200 with `newly_resumed: false`.

get.description: Per-shard status of the audit-record export to an external SIEM sink (issue #953): cursor position, delivery lag, delivery state, and the last sink error. Admin-gated: it reports the completeness posture of the privileged-action log, which is exactly what an attacker would want to know before acting. It never returns audit record CONTENTS -- use `GET /audit` for those.

200.description: `sink_configured` reports ONLY whether the process serving this request has an audit sink installed. It is not a fleet-wide signal and must not be diagnosed from: in a split web/worker deployment an API process legitimately reports false while export is healthy on the worker fleet, and true would not establish that the process actually running the scanner is configured. The database-backed signals -- `pending_records` growing across two reads, `lag_seconds` rising, or a persistent NOT_STARTED -- describe the shard rather than whichever process answered. Each entry in `shards` carries {shard, cursor_seq, last_assigned_seq, pending_records, lag_seconds, delivery_state, consecutive_failures, last_status, last_error, last_delivered_at, next_attempt_at}. `cursor_seq` is the highest per-shard export sequence the sink has acknowledged: every record at or below it has been delivered at least once. `lag_seconds` is the age of the OLDEST unacknowledged record (not the newest -- under sustained load a stuck exporter always has a brand-new unexported record, so a newest-based lag would read ~0 during exactly the outage that matters). `delivery_state` is one of IDLE, DELIVERING, BACKOFF, RETRYING, RETIRED, or NOT_STARTED; NOT_STARTED means no exporter has ever claimed that shard, and the entry still reports the live backlog it would face. RETIRED means an operator ran decommission_cursor: the cursor row survives only to preserve the sequence high-water mark, no exporter owes the shard records, and retention may purge them, so the entry's other fields are a frozen snapshot rather than live state. An unreachable shard degrades the response to `status: "partial"` (naming it in `unavailable_shards`) rather than failing the whole read.

post.description: Retire one shard's audit-export cursor, permitting retention to purge its aged audit records (issue #953, issue #1273). This is the audited front door for what used to be a bare library call with no route, no auth gate, and no audit trail at all -- retirement discards the compliance guarantee over any record the shard has not yet shipped, so an auditor must be able to name who authorised that. The retirement and its audit record (`audit_export.decommission`) are one transaction on one connection, on the target shard's own connection, exactly like the redrive route. A shard already retired, or never configured, changes nothing but is still audited: an auditor needs the record of the request, not only of requests that had an effect.

shard.description: Shard whose export cursor to retire.

200.description: `outcome` is `retired` on a genuine transition, or `already_retired` when the shard was already retired (a no-op that is still audited). Retiring bumps the shard's claim epoch and clears its lease, so a delivery already in flight cannot acknowledge over the retirement -- the same fencing the redrive route uses.

404.description: The named shard has no audit-export cursor: audit export has never run there.

503.description: Harvest storage is not configured, the named shard is unreachable, or the audit record for this decommission could not be written. The retirement and its audit record commit together, so a 503 from the audit write means the cursor was NOT retired.

post.summary: Retire one shard's audit-export cursor, permitting retention to purge its aged audit records (issue #953, issue #1273).

post.description: Reactivate one shard's retired audit-export cursor, resuming from the preserved sequence high-water mark (issue #1273). The inverse of `POST /admin/audit-export/decommission`, audited the same way. Resuming export used to happen as an implicit side effect of the exporter's next scanner tick, which raced a concurrent decommission and left no record of who decided to resume it; `ensure_cursor_row` no longer reactivates a retired cursor under any circumstance, so this route is now the only way back from `RETIRED` to live.

shard.description: Shard whose export cursor to reactivate.

200.description: `outcome` is `reactivated` on a genuine transition, or `already_active` when the shard was already live (a no-op that is still audited). New records continue the preserved sequence rather than restarting at 0, so a receiver deduping on `(shard, seq)` never sees a reused pair naming a different record.

404.description: The named shard has no audit-export cursor: audit export has never run there.

503.description: Harvest storage is not configured, the named shard is unreachable, or the audit record for this reactivation could not be written. The reactivation and its audit record commit together, so a 503 from the audit write means the cursor was NOT reactivated.

post.summary: Reactivate one shard's retired audit-export cursor, resuming from the preserved sequence high-water mark (issue #1273).
post.x-harvest-idempotency: Idempotent in effect: the cursor ends up active. A repeat call reports `already_active` rather than erroring, and still writes its own audit record.

post.description: Rewind one shard's audit-export cursor so already-delivered audit records are re-exported to the SIEM sink (issue #953), for recovery after sink-side data loss. Re-exported records are byte-identical -- the per-record export sequence is never re-stamped, so a record carries the same (shard, seq) and the same JSON on every delivery and the receiver dedupes on that pair. A cursor may only ever move BACKWARDS: a request that would move it forward, or leave it where it is, is refused with 400 rather than applied, because advancing it would mark records delivered that never were. The `before` form resolves to one below the LOWEST sequence assigned to a record at or after that instant, so any clock/commit-order skew makes the rewind reach further back (costing duplicate deliveries the receiver dedupes) rather than skipping records. The redrive itself writes an audit record (`audit_export.redrive`) in the same transaction as the rewind, so re-exporting is as auditable as the operations being exported.

before.description: RFC 3339 instant; rewind so every audit record that occurred at or after it re-exports. Exactly one of to_seq or before must be supplied.

shard.description: Shard whose export cursor to rewind.

to_seq.description: Rewind to this exact export sequence; records with seq > to_seq re-export. Exactly one of to_seq or before must be supplied. A negative value is clamped to 0 (re-export everything still retained).

200.description: `outcome` is `rewound`. `from` is where the cursor was, `to` where it now is; records with seq > to will be re-delivered by the exporter on its next tick. The rewind also bumps the shard's claim epoch and clears its lease, so a delivery already in flight when the rewind lands cannot acknowledge over it and silently undo the redrive. The rewind and the `audit_export.redrive` audit record are one transaction on one connection, so an applied-but-unaudited redrive is not representable; that audit row lands in the TARGET shard's audit log (not the default shard's, unlike other audited routes) because it describes a shard-scoped mutation and a second connection could neither be atomic with the rewind nor safely acquired while holding it. and the audit row's target_id records the shard AND the requested position (`shard=0;to_seq=42`), since a redrive is the one operation here that can trigger a mass re-export.

400.description: Neither or both of to_seq/before supplied, or the request would not move the cursor backwards -- it is at or above the current position (the message reports both the current cursor and the requested one). Advancing a cursor would mark records delivered that never were.

404.description: The named shard has no LIVE audit-export cursor: export has either never run there, or has been retired with decommission_cursor. A retired shard is refused rather than rewound -- retention no longer protects its records and no exporter is running to ship them, so reporting a successful rewind would be a promise the system cannot keep.

503.description: Harvest storage is not configured, the named shard is unreachable, or the audit record for this redrive could not be written. The rewind and its audit record commit together, so a 503 from the audit write means the cursor was NOT moved.

post.summary: Rewind one shard's audit-export cursor so already-delivered audit records are re-exported to the SIEM sink (issue #953), for recovery after sink-side data loss.
post.x-harvest-idempotency: Idempotent in effect: the cursor ends up at the requested position. A repeat of the same request is refused with 400 rather than applied a second time, because a request that would not move the cursor BACKWARDS (at or above the current position) is never applied. Each accepted call writes its own audit record.

get.description: Report payload-codec key rotation progress per shard (issue #948). Lists every registered codec key id, which one is active for new writes, and -- per shard -- how many harvest_events rows still carry each key id plus the lazy re-encryption sweep's durable resume cursor. This is the screen an operator watches to know when an outgoing key has zero remaining rows. A zero census is NECESSARY but NOT SUFFICIENT for retirement: it proves no row references the key right now on the shards this process can reach, not that no worker is still encoding under it and no already-encoded append is still in flight. Retirement additionally requires an attested fleet write fence -- see the procedure in docs/operations/codec-key-rotation.md. Treating zero here as authorization to destroy key material can leave a late-committing row permanently unreadable. Admin-gated: the body names operator-chosen key identifiers and exposes the encryption posture of stored history. It carries NO key material and NO payload content.

200.description: Each entry in `shards` is {shard_id, rows_by_key_id, rows_remaining, cursor}. `rows_by_key_id` maps every observed codec key id to the number of rows referencing it on that shard; rows written before key ids existed carry no `kid` and are counted under the designated legacy key id ("legacy"). `rows_remaining` is the sum over NON-active key ids -- the number that must reach zero before that key can be retired. `cursor` is {last_event_id, rows_reencrypted, completed_at, updated_at} for the active key's sweep pass, or null before the first batch runs; it is keyed on (shard, active key id), so flipping the active key starts a fresh pass. An unreachable shard degrades the response to `status: "partial"` and is named in `unavailable_shards`; `rows_remaining_total` is then a LOWER BOUND, not a count -- an unread shard's rows are unknown, never zero. The retirement gate applies the same fail-closed rule and refuses to retire a key while any expected shard is unreadable. On a deployment with no keyed codecs registered -- every deployment that has not adopted key rotation -- `registered_key_ids` is empty, `active_key_id` is the legacy sentinel, and every count is zero.

get.description: List every currently-paused task queue (issue #619), with the reason for the hold, the operator who placed it, when it was placed, and how many PENDING tasks it is holding. Cross-shard: a shard-scoped pause lists with its `scope_shard_id`, and an unreachable shard degrades the response to `status: "partial"` (naming it in `unavailable_shards`) rather than failing the whole read.

200.description: Each entry in paused_queues carries queue_name, held_task_count (summed across shards), provenance_uniform, effective_scope, and a shards array of per-shard objects {shard_id, reason, paused_by, paused_at, scope_shard_id, held_task_count}. The top-level reason/paused_by/paused_at/scope_shard_id summarise the EARLIEST hold. Because pause is idempotent and preserves the original provenance on a re-pause, a fleet-wide hold landing over a pre-existing shard-scoped hold (or two independent scoped holds) can leave shards disagreeing; provenance_uniform is false in that case and the shards array carries each shard's own story. Uniformity compares reason/paused_by/scope_shard_id and deliberately not paused_at, since each shard stamps its own NOW(). effective_scope ("fleet" | "partial_fleet" | "shard") reports what the hold ACTUALLY covers, derived from the shards that hold the queue versus the expected shard set (every pool plus every shard the router knows about) -- distinct from scope_shard_id, which records only the INTENT of the request that wrote each row. A fleet-wide pause that reached only some shards persists scope_shard_id = NULL on the shards it reached and no row at all on the ones it missed, so intent alone cannot distinguish it from a complete hold while the missed shards keep dispatching; effective_scope is "partial_fleet" in that case (re-issue the pause). An unreachable shard counts as expected-but-not-holding -- the safe direction, since it may still be dispatching -- so a partial read also reports "partial_fleet".

200.description: Each entry in ineligible_workers carries a nested reason_codes array explaining why that online worker cannot claim the queue's tasks. The full taxonomy (issue #611): wrong_queue_subscription, wrong_shard_assignment, worker_draining, worker_stopped, build_incompatible, sticky_owned_by_other_worker, concurrency_saturated (a per-key concurrency cap is actually saturated), rate_limit_exhausted (the task's rate-limit bucket has < 1.0 token; renamed from the earlier rate_limit_saturated), circuit_open (the task's next activity is gated by an OPEN circuit breaker — a downstream outage tripped it), circuit_half_open (the breaker is testing recovery with a single in-flight probe; the explainer's non-mutating snapshot reports circuit_open through the cooldown and only observes half_open once a probe dispatch is admitted), queue_paused (an operator holds the task's whole queue — issue #619), activity_paused (an operator holds the task's activity type fleet-wide — issue #807; reported only for task_type='activity' rows, matching the claim gate, so a workflow task carrying the 'mixed_signal_suspension' sentinel in activity_name is never reported held), and unsatisfied_requirement:{key}={value} / unsatisfied_requirement:{key} in [{values}] for capability mismatches. For a CB activity that also declares a rate limit, rate limiting is enforced at dispatch (issue #369) so its impediment surfaces as circuit_open/circuit_half_open, never a stale rate_limit_exhausted. Multiple applicable codes are all listed. The deliberate operator holds (activity_paused, queue_paused) lead the array — a pause reorders the reasons, it never suppresses a co-occurring impediment — and the remainder is alphabetical so the array is stable across polls.

post.description: Hold dispatch on a named task queue during a scoped downstream outage (issue #619). While paused, no worker claims NEW tasks from the queue; held tasks stay PENDING and are never failed, retried, or dead-lettered, and an already-RUNNING task finishes naturally. The relative `schedule_to_start` timer is suspended for held tasks; the absolute `schedule_to_close` deadline (issue #378) keeps ticking, so a long hold can still time out work carrying one — a pause is not an SLA extension. Idempotent: re-pausing an already-paused queue is a 200 no-op that preserves the original reason and operator (`newly_paused: false`). The operator `reason` is truncated to 500 characters at the API boundary. A partially-applied fleet-wide hold is reported as 207, not 200 — see the success-response notes. Admin only; audited as `queue.pause`, including rejected attempts.

Leading or trailing whitespace is rejected with a 400 rather than trimmed: queue names are stored verbatim at enqueue time, so `"payments "` and `"payments"` are two genuinely distinct, independently reachable queues and trimming would silently hold the wrong one while reporting success. Send the exact name. Interior whitespace is allowed.

200.description: A hold applied to only SOME target shards returns 207 Multi-Status with `ok: false` and `status: "partial"`, plus a `partial_failures` string naming the shards that were not reached (including a shard the router knows about but this process has no pool for). The hold is NOT in effect fleet-wide in that case — the missed shards keep dispatching — so re-issue the request (it is idempotent). A fully applied request returns 200 with `ok: true` and `status: "complete"`, and omits `partial_failures`. Cross-shard provenance: `held_task_count` is the fleet-wide sum, while the top-level `reason`/`paused_by`/`paused_at`/`scope_shard_id` describe the EARLIEST hold (tie-broken by shard id — the same rule `GET /admin/queues/paused` and the Vantage banner use, so the three surfaces never disagree). Because an idempotent re-pause preserves each shard's ORIGINAL provenance, a fleet-wide request landing over pre-existing scoped holds leaves the shards disagreeing: `shards` then carries every shard's own `{shard_id, newly_paused, reason, paused_by, paused_at, scope_shard_id, held_task_count}` and `provenance_uniform` is false. `provenance_uniform` compares `(reason, paused_by, scope_shard_id)` and deliberately NOT `paused_at`, since each shard stamps its own NOW().

post.description: Release an operator queue pause (issue #619). Held tasks become immediately claimable again, and the time each task spent held is credited back to its `scheduled_at` so the thaw does not retroactively schedule-to-start-time-out the whole backlog. Body is optional; a bare POST resumes fleet-wide. `released_reason`/`released_paused_by` echo the provenance of the hold that was released — the pause row is deleted by the resume, so this is the last moment the *why* is recoverable. Idempotent: resuming a queue that is not paused is a 200 no-op (`newly_resumed: false`). A partially-applied resume is reported as 207, not 200. Admin only; audited as `queue.resume`, including rejected attempts.

get.description: Read-only companion to the SET/DELETE routes above (issue #945): resolves and reports a workflow's TTL'd pacing-override state directly against the bucket the token-consumption path actually reads, independent of whether the workflow currently has any deferred-start backlog. GET /admin/start-throttle only surfaces override state for a workflow while it has pending backlog rows; this route answers reliably even when the backlog has fully drained but the override is still running for the rest of its TTL, or before any pressure has occurred at all. Buckets are shard-local (issue #607/#247); the top-level 200/207 body reports whichever reachable shard has a LIVE override whenever any shard does -- never the mere fewest-remaining-tokens row, since raw token count says nothing about whether an operator override is active (issue #945 review, round 4, P2). A read reaching only SOME shards, OR one where reachable shards genuinely disagree on override state, is reported as 207, not 200 -- see the success-response notes.

Millisecond clock skew on override_expires_at alone across a normal successful multi-shard SET does not count as disagreement. `shards` is present whenever the response is 207 (both the shard-outage and the disagreement case) and lists every REACHABLE shard's own view (shard IDs named only in shard_errors are omitted, since their row could not be read). A fully reachable, fully agreeing read returns plain 200 and omits shard_errors/shard_disagreement/shards.

200.description: Each entry in ineligible_workers carries a nested reason_codes array explaining why that online worker cannot claim the task. The full taxonomy (issue #611): wrong_queue_subscription, wrong_shard_assignment, worker_draining, worker_stopped, build_incompatible, sticky_owned_by_other_worker, concurrency_saturated (a per-key concurrency cap is actually saturated), rate_limit_exhausted (the task's rate-limit bucket has < 1.0 token; renamed from the earlier rate_limit_saturated), circuit_open (the task's next activity is gated by an OPEN circuit breaker — a downstream outage tripped it), circuit_half_open (the breaker is testing recovery with a single in-flight probe; the explainer's non-mutating snapshot reports circuit_open through the cooldown and only observes half_open once a probe dispatch is admitted), queue_paused (an operator holds the task's whole queue — issue #619), activity_paused (an operator holds the task's activity type fleet-wide — issue #807; reported only for task_type='activity' rows, matching the claim gate, so a workflow task carrying the 'mixed_signal_suspension' sentinel in activity_name is never reported held), and unsatisfied_requirement:{key}={value} / unsatisfied_requirement:{key} in [{values}] for capability mismatches. For a CB activity that also declares a rate limit, rate limiting is enforced at dispatch (issue #369) so its impediment surfaces as circuit_open/circuit_half_open, never a stale rate_limit_exhausted. Multiple applicable codes are all listed. The deliberate operator holds (activity_paused, queue_paused) lead the array — a pause reorders the reasons, it never suppresses a co-occurring impediment — and the remainder is alphabetical so the array is stable across polls.

get.description: Historical per-tenant/per-workflow usage report (issue #596): the historical companion to the point-in-time GET /admin/concurrency endpoint. Aggregates already-durable data (harvest_workflow_executions + harvest_events) over a required [from, to] window, grouped by workflow_name (default) or a search_attr:<key> tenant key, fanned out and summed across every shard. workflow_starts counts by started_at in the window; completed/failed/cancelled/timed_out count by completed_at in the window and matching terminal state; activity_executions counts ActivityStarted events (one per dispatch attempt) in the window; activity_executions_failed counts terminal ActivityFailed/ActivityTimedOut events in the window; activity_compute_seconds sums each activity's final-attempt start-to-terminal wall-clock span for terminal events in the window. Local and externally-completed activities are excluded (no ActivityStarted event). Executions lacking the requested search_attr key are grouped under the literal group "(unattributed)" rather than dropped. An unreachable shard is named in unavailable_shards rather than failing the call wholesale. A malformed percent-encoded query-string byte sequence (an invalid UTF-8 byte, or an incomplete/non-hex `%` escape) is rejected with a 400 before any parameter is parsed, rather than silently substituting the Unicode replacement character and proceeding with a wrong-but-plausible value (issue #1151, sweeping the issue #774 `queue-coverage` fix to every other raw-pairs route).

post.description: Force-fail exactly one hung in-flight (RUNNING) activity task. Appends ActivityFailed with the distinct error_type 'OperatorForceFailed' through the existing recording path (no new event variant), marks the task row FAILED with the typed failure envelope, and wakes the parked workflow task so the owning workflow advances to its own failure/compensation path -- it is NOT terminated. Remaining retry attempts are skipped regardless of retry policy (the forced failure is non-retryable by construction), and a late result from the worker still running the activity is ignored (no double-apply). Only RUNNING activity tasks of a non-terminal execution are force-failable. Note: if the owning workflow has a workflow-level retry policy (issue #523) and propagates this error to workflow failure, the run is retried fresh and the activity re-dispatched -- use cancel/terminate instead if the goal is to stop the run. Local activities run inline and have no task-queue row -- this endpoint does not apply to them (404).

get.description: Open-awaitables diagnostic (issue #615): names every open awaitable the execution is currently parked on, across six categories — pending activities (regular/local/external), unfired durable timers, awaited-but-unfulfilled signals (by name), pending child workflows (name + child exec id), unresolved await_condition parks, and pending updates — plus mutex acquires (#691) and external-workflow operations (#757) when present. The wait-set is derived by replaying recorded history read-only to the current suspension point (the #612 drive machinery), so it sees awaited-but-ABSENT inputs the side tables cannot (an unsent signal, a never-true condition). Each awaitable carries kind, name/identifier, a since timestamp derived from recorded history, and a deadline where one applies (timer fire time, signal/child race deadline, external schedule-to-close, activity schedule-to-close/start-to-close from the task row). Payload-free: names, ids, and timestamps only — never inputs/payloads/update args — so read-path payload decoding (issue #608) is deliberately skipped. Admin-gated (the eligibility endpoints' posture). Terminal executions return 200 with an empty awaitables list and wait_set = "terminal". Each category is bounded to the first category_cap entries with overflow reported in truncated/truncated_kinds. When the replay drive is unavailable (handler not registered on this node, classic DAG, encrypted history without decode, replay timeout/panic, a detected replay divergence, or a replay that reaches terminal on a non-terminal run), wait_set degrades to "history_only" with wait_set_reason naming why — activities/timers/children/updates still report from the event-log scan, but awaited-unsent signals and await_condition parks are not observable in that mode. Read path is shard-local (routed via the exec id's embedded shard); no cross-shard fan-out. Appends no events, performs no writes, adds no new WorkflowEvent variant.

get.description: Per-execution stall diagnosis (issue #809): answers "is this run healthily waiting or pathologically stuck, and what is the actionable root cause?" in one call, replacing the 4+ endpoint correlation an operator does by hand today. Returns a one-word triage `health` (`healthy` | `stalled` | `degraded` | `blocked_external` | `terminal`), a discriminated `blocked_on` object, and `last_event_age_seconds`. `blocked_on` is internally tagged on `type` (snake_case) and closed over: `healthy_in_progress`; `awaiting_signal` {signal_name, since?}; `sleeping_timer` {fires_at}; `pending_child` {child_exec_id, child_state}; `activity_retrying` {activity_name, attempt, last_error?, next_attempt_at?}; `activity_deferred` {activity_name?, next_attempt_at}; `activity_no_worker` {queue, activity_name?}; `activity_circuit_open` {activity_name, phase, forced_open, cooldown_until?} (`phase` is `open` | `half_open`: a half-open breaker admits a probe right now and closes on success, so its `health` is `healthy` (and `forced_open` is always `false`, since a forced-open breaker's phase never leaves `open` until an explicit force-close); an `open` breaker with `forced_open: false` was tripped organically and self-heals on its own cooldown timer with no operator action, but issue #369's non-retryable `ActivityFailure::circuit_open` fast-fails every dispatch until then -- the activity is heading for a terminal failure, not progress, so its `health` is `degraded`, not `healthy` and not `stalled`; an `open` breaker with `forced_open: true` was operator-forced -- no probe is admitted on any timer -- and needs an explicit force-close, so its `health` is `stalled` (issue #1193). `forced_open` is the AUTHORITATIVE discriminator, sourced directly from the in-process registry's own flag -- NOT inferred from whether `cooldown_until` is present (issue #1193 Codex round-1 P2 on PR #1365): a policy cooldown configured outside `chrono`'s representable range makes an organically-tripped breaker ALSO report `cooldown_until` absent, which would be indistinguishable from a forced-open one by that field alone; `cooldown_until` remains present only as an informational display deadline when it can be computed. An organic trip whose `cooldown_until` is at or before the row's own EFFECTIVE dispatch instant (`max(now, scheduled_at)` -- `now` for an already-due row, since it could be attempted any moment) does NOT report `activity_circuit_open` at all (issue #1193 Codex round-4/round-5 P2): `CircuitBreakerRegistry::on_dispatch` checks the elapsed cooldown at the actual dispatch instant, so this row's own future attempt is what would be admitted as the recovery probe rather than fast-failed, and the row instead reports the ordinary `activity_retrying` / `activity_deferred` (or, for an already-due, otherwise-unimpeded row, `healthy_in_progress`) it would without a breaker in the way. A forced-open breaker has no cooldown to compare against and is unaffected by this exception. The comparison uses a wall-clock timestamp captured back-to-back with the breaker snapshot read, not the (potentially much earlier, pre-database-query) `now` the rest of the diagnosis is timestamped with, so the derived `cooldown_until` does not systematically underestimate the true deadline. In a fan-out containing any two of the three circuit shapes, the more severe one outranks the less severe one in the precedence ladder below (forced-open > organic-open > half-open), so the genuinely actionable stall is never masked by a self-healing or already-recovering one purely because of row order -- forced vs organic was Codex round-1 P1 on PR #1365, organic vs half-open was Codex round-2 P1 on the same PR: the two used to share a tier while also sharing a health value, so a tie was harmless until `Degraded` split them apart); `activity_rate_limited` {key, activity_name?}; `activity_rate_limit_bucket_missing` {key, activity_name?} (the bucket row does not exist, so the claim gate's `EXISTS` refuses it forever -- `stalled`, unlike the refilling `activity_rate_limited`); `activity_concurrency_deferred` {key, activity_name?}; `activity_queue_paused` {queue, activity_name?}; `activity_paused` {activity_name} (an operator paused the activity TYPE (#807), so claim_task's paused_activities anti-join holds it on every queue on the shard -- distinct from the queue-wide activity_queue_paused, and ranked just under it because the queue pause is the broader lever); `awaiting_external_handoff` {token, activity_name?}; `paused` {actor?, since?}; `non_determinism_blocked` {since, reason?, block_count}; `awaiting_replay_wait` {wait_kind, name?, since?}; `workflow_no_worker` {queue}; `workflow_queue_paused` {queue}; `timer_overdue{fires_at,overdue_by_seconds}`, `no_pending_work`. Optional members are omitted, never null. Correlates, in a single shard-local read: the pending stack, per-queue worker liveness (the canonical #774 worker_covers_queue predicate, so it cannot drift from /admin/queue-coverage) -- a PENDING row asks whether any worker can claim it right now (Active only, since a Draining worker claims nothing new), while a HELD row asks whether its own recorded claimant is still alive (Active OR Draining, because a worker that has begun a graceful shutdown still runs its held work to completion) plus the row's own claim gates -- required build (#171/#604), required capabilities (#804) and session pin (#606), each evaluated against the SAME worker; an activity row with NO required_capabilities snapshot (a legacy or manual enqueue) is still gated by its REGISTERED handler's requires, mirroring claim_task's ineligible-activities gate, so an un-snapshotted row no worker can claim is reported as a stall rather than as healthy progress, the in-process circuit registry (#369, consulted via list() only -- never on_dispatch/force_* -- so diagnosing can never advance a breaker's phase; and because that registry is per worker PROCESS, its phase is reported only when this API replica's own co-located worker is the SOLE worker that could claim the row, since a peer replica whose breaker is closed can still dispatch it -- a fleet-wide outage is therefore deliberately under-reported rather than risking a false stall, and /admin/circuits per replica remains the authoritative per-breaker surface), rate-limit bucket and per-key concurrency saturation (shaped exactly like claim_task's own gates; a circuit-breaker-tracked activity's bucket is never itself the claim-time impediment regardless of build, since the breaker gates it at dispatch instead (#369) -- but THIS replica's tracked/untracked fact about an activity is an in-process compile-time declaration, and whether it can be trusted for a given row is build-scoped (#1190): both activity_rate_limited and activity_rate_limit_bucket_missing are reported only when every worker eligible to claim the row shares this replica's build, so during a rolling deploy an eligible peer on a different build -- which may declare the breaker differently in EITHER direction, tracked here but not there or vice versa -- never has a rate-limit verdict fabricated for it, the same unknown-worker-is-assumed-capable rule the circuit registry follows above), the operator queue-pause table (#619), and the task row's own attempt/error/scheduled_at retry timing. Every activity row is classified and the WORST by a fixed cross-task precedence ladder wins (queue_paused, then activity_paused, no_worker, rate_limit_bucket_missing, circuit_open[forced_open: true], circuit_open[forced_open: false, phase: open], circuit_open[phase: half_open], concurrency_deferred, rate_limited, retrying, deferred, healthy), so one wedged slot in a wide fan-out is never masked by a milder sibling -- including a forced-open breaker never being masked by an organically-tripped one (issue #1193 Codex round-1 P1) and an organically-tripped breaker never being masked by a half-open one (issue #1193 Codex round-2 P1) at a different activity in the same fan-out. ONE exception to "the activity bucket always wins over the workflow task" (issue #1193 Codex round-3 P1): when the winning activity verdict resolves to health degraded specifically, and the run's OWN workflow task cannot be claimed at all (workflow_no_worker or workflow_queue_paused), THAT is reported instead -- a frozen decision cycle is worse than one activity self-resolving into a failure, and unlike every other activity health this one carries no such guarantee on its own. Every other activity health (stalled, blocked_external, healthy) keeps the pre-existing, deliberately-activity-first behavior unchanged. Within a single row the three non-self-healing gates (queue_paused, no_worker, circuit_open) are checked first, then the not-yet-due branch, then the two self-healing gates: a task that is not yet due has not reached the claim gates at all, so reporting a momentarily-saturated bucket would drop the attempt/last_error/next_attempt_at an operator needs. A future scheduled_at alone does NOT mean failed-and-retrying -- the dispatcher also pushes a task forward with no failure at all (dispatch-time rate-limit deferral, which even decrements the claim-time attempt back down, plus session-capacity and capability-miss redelivery), so the not-yet-due branch reports activity_retrying only when there is failure evidence (a recorded error, which a later deferral never clears) and activity_deferred otherwise. A claimed (RUNNING) row is healthy only while a live worker still polls its queue -- a claimed row whose fleet is gone is a poison-pill orphan (#367), not progress. health is derived from the verdict class alone and never from event age, so a long durable sleep reports healthy no matter how old its last event is. contributing_reason_codes is the UNION of every claim-time impediment across ALL of the execution's activity rows -- not just the row blocked_on names -- so a lower-ranked cause is never hidden behind a higher-ranked sibling in a fan-out; it is sourced verbatim from the eligibility explainer's own pure task_intrinsic_impediment_reasons (#611) so the single-verdict and multi-reason surfaces cannot drift in how a cause is named. Worker liveness is the one reason that is NOT a claim-time gate, so it is reported for a HELD row too -- but keyed on the same question the verdict asks: a PENDING row on claim eligibility (an Active worker could claim it), a HELD row on its own recorded claimant's liveness (Active OR Draining). Without that split the codes contradict the verdict in both directions -- a row held by a live draining claimant would report healthy yet carry no_live_worker, and an orphan held by a dead claimant would OMIT it whenever a live Active peer happens to cover the queue. An awaited-but-unsent signal is visible only to the #615 replay drive, which is comparatively expensive and ranks below activities/handoffs/children, so it is consulted ONLY when the database-observable categories would otherwise resolve to sleeping_timer or no_pending_work -- wait_set reports replayed, history_only (with wait_set_reason: an upstream reason such as handler_not_registered passed through verbatim, else wait_set_unavailable when the replay errors, wait_set_timed_out when it exceeds the query timeout, or execution_went_terminal on a TOCTOU race) or not_consulted accordingly; the replay is bounded by the server's query timeout; the verdict is identical either way and the common wedged-activity path never pays for a replay. Every OTHER awaitable kind replay can name -- a command-less ctx.await_condition park, a durable mutex acquire (#691), an admitted update awaiting its handler, a parked external-workflow operation (#492/#757/#751) -- leaves no row in any side table this endpoint reads, so replay is the only source that can see it; those report awaiting_replay_wait (blocked_external) naming the kind. They are consulted BELOW every side-table cause, so they can only ever replace what would otherwise be a false no_pending_work and can never mask a more precise verdict such as sleeping_timer. Below every category above sits the run's OWN workflow task row (task_type = 'workflow'), consulted purely as a fallback so it can never mask a real cause: a held claim means the handler is executing this instant (healthy_in_progress -- the shape a long local activity holds while scheduling no queue row at all) but ONLY while a live worker still polls its queue, since a claim left behind by a crashed worker is a poison-pill orphan (#367) and reports workflow_no_worker; a PENDING row means the decision cycle is awaiting dispatch and is classified by the same hard-impediment-first ladder an activity row uses -- workflow_queue_paused when an operator holds that queue, then workflow_no_worker (the workflow-task analogue of the no-live-worker stall) when nothing polls it, which outranks a not-yet-due dispatcher deferral on purpose because, unlike a timed sleep, a deferral only self-heals if something claims the row when the timestamp arrives, then healthy_in_progress; and a parked row (RUNNING with a NULL worker, which advances on a wake rather than a claim) is left to the lost-task verdict unchanged. A terminal execution returns health = terminal with terminal_outcome and NO blocked_on. Payload-free apart from the task row's own error text: names, ids, timestamps and queue/bucket keys only -- never an activity input, signal payload or output. That one error string IS routed through read-path payload decoding (#608), exactly as /stack routes the same column for its own last_failure, so an admin never reads plaintext there and a ciphertext envelope here. Admin-gated (the eligibility endpoints' posture: the body names queue, rate-limit and concurrency keys plus fleet coverage state). Shard-local: routed O(1) from the exec id's embedded shard, no cross-shard fan-out. An unfired durable timer more than 60s past its deadline reports timer_overdue (stalled) rather than a healthy sleep -- but ONLY when that timer actually owns the workflow's wake. Timers fire when a worker claims the owning workflow task, and only persist_started_timer reschedules that task to the deadline; every *_park path (signal wait, mutex acquire, activity wait, scheduled activities, child workflows, external handoff) discards the armed deadline and parks the task on the thing being awaited, so a timer armed alongside one of those goes overdue as a matter of course and fires on that wait's completion wake. The verdict is therefore gated on the task row itself -- a claimed or parked row means some other wake owns the run, so the more precise handoff/child/signal cause is reported instead, and only a PENDING row long past its own scheduled_at is a genuinely missed timer wake. Conversely, a durable side-table wait does not advance on its own either: a timer fires only when a worker claims the owning workflow task, so a HARD impediment on that task -- an operator queue pause (#619) or no live poller -- outranks every timer verdict and reports workflow_queue_paused / workflow_no_worker, naming the queue an operator must fix rather than a sleep that can never end. Only the hard impediments are hoisted; the task row's ordinary healthy-dispatch result stays a fallback so it never masks the more specific sleeping_timer. It is checked BELOW the activity bucket on purpose (a wedged activity names the specific thing to fix); ranking it above the handoff/child/signal categories is harmless by construction, because every one of those parks the workflow task and a parked row is not awaiting a claim. When replay diverges, the engine BLOCKS the run (#603) rather than failing it: the execution stays RUNNING and its workflow task is re-pended at a capped-exponential backoff INDEFINITELY, which by row shape alone is identical to an ordinary dispatcher deferral -- so a permanently wedged run would otherwise report healthy_in_progress. The execution row's own nd_blocked_at is authoritative and reports non_determinism_blocked (stalled) carrying the recorded divergence, the block instant and the re-fire count. It is ranked directly under paused because it is the same class of fact -- an explicit state the engine stamped on the execution row, not an inference from a liveness proxy -- and it outranks every side-table cause because the block re-fires on EVERY decision cycle regardless of what those rows are doing; nothing is lost, since a pending activity's own impediments still reach the operator through contributing_reason_codes, which is a union across rows rather than the winner's reasons. paused stays above it, mirroring the engine: a pause observed under the row lock supersedes the block and re-parks instead. Appends no WorkflowEvent, performs no task-queue mutation, adds no migration -- safe to call repeatedly.

post.description: Tombstone all payload-bearing fields (input, output, payload, details, value, last_completion_result) in every event row, the execution row, and signal rows for a terminal workflow execution. Cascades to terminal child executions on the same shard. Requires the execution to be in a terminal state (COMPLETED, FAILED, CANCELLED, TIMED_OUT, CONTINUED_AS_NEW, or TERMINATED). Scrubs EVERY shard that still holds a copy of the execution: a shard rebalance (issue #964) seals rather than deletes the source, so a rebalanced run's payloads live on both the live target and the sealed source until the source shard's retention collects it, and each additional residence that was scrubbed is reported in the response's prior_residences array. The terminal-state and legal-hold gates are evaluated against the LIVE residence only, so a still-running execution can never be erased through its own sealed shadow. A residence whose copy has already been collected contributes nothing and is not an error; a residence this node cannot reach fails the whole call, because an erasure that cannot be shown to be complete must not be reported as complete. The one exception is a RETIRED shard -- decommissioned, its pool removed fleet-wide and its ids forwarded to a successor per docs/runbooks/shard-decommission.md, which requires its payloads to be destroyed or erased before the forward is declared. Those are listed in retired_residences rather than failing the call, since failing closed on them would make every run that ever lived on a retired shard permanently un-erasable.

post.description: Replay ONE execution's recorded history against the currently-registered #[workflow] handler on this node and return a structured determinism verdict (issue #614). POST is used instead of GET because it drives a replay of the workflow function; this route never writes workflow events and performs no writes (read-only, admin-gated). The DB connection is dropped before user code is driven, and the replay is pure in-memory replay. Answers 'will — or did — this run diverge under the code deployed right now?': useful for a PAUSED or non-determinism-blocked RUNNING run (the divergence object mirrors the #603 block diagnostic: kind/event_index/expected/actual), or a terminal FAILED run for retroactive forensics. The verdict is one of: clean (message 'no divergence under current code'), diverged (with a divergence object), workflow_failed (with a failure object), not_registered (the workflow type is not registered on this node), or not_replayable_dag (a classic DAG is not on the replay path). Since issue #952 a terminal FAILED run whose history REPRODUCES its recorded failure under the current code is 'clean' (reproducing a recorded failure is not a divergence) and carries that error in the failure object, with message 'no divergence under current code; the recorded failure was reproduced'; 'workflow_failed' remains for a replay that failed where the recorded history did not. All five verdicts return 200 — the diagnosis, not the HTTP status, carries the answer. The replay runs in canary mode, so a healthy in-flight run parked mid-flight (a PAUSED/RUNNING frontier suspension) is correctly reported clean rather than a false diverged; a terminal run externally sealed mid-await (TIMED_OUT/cancelled/terminated) is likewise clean. The replay is bounded by WorkerConfig::query_timeout; the query_timeout bound applies to async-yielding replays, and a workflow that busy-loops synchronously without ever awaiting is out of scope, exactly as for the live executor.

post.description: Re-run a terminal workflow execution: start a BRAND-NEW execution from the source run's recorded start parameters. When the re-run reuses the source's business key (the default), the source row is SEALED to CONTINUED_AS_NEW so the business key is free for the new run — its recorded prior state is returned as source_prior_state, and its output/error/completed_at are preserved untouched. Admin-only. Provenance on the new run is start_source='rerun', start_source_ref=<source execution id>, started_by=<actor>. Cloned verbatim from the source row: input (unless overridden), queue, memo, search attributes (minus the six replay-non-determinism diagnostic keys), execution timeout, chain timeout, SLA, owner/runbook_url/severity, context headers, workflow retry policy, and completion callbacks. NOT preserved: priority (it is not stored on the execution row), and schedule provenance (schedule_id / scheduled_for / origin are cleared, matching the reset-fork precedent — an operator intervention is deliberately excluded from scheduled carryover). The new run always begins a fresh continue-as-new chain and a fresh retry chain (attempt 1).

get.description: Server-Sent Events stream of the EPHEMERAL live-output progress chunks a running workflow publishes via ctx.publish_progress (issue #791). Chunks are ordered over Postgres LISTEN/NOTIFY with sub-second delivery. This is a best-effort side channel: chunks are never recorded in harvest_events, never replayed, and there is NO backfill on (re)connect — a subscriber that connects after a chunk was published will not see it (chunk content may be non-deterministic precisely because it is never stored). Each SSE message carries id (a monotonic, epoch-prefixed seq — a gap means a missed chunk) plus event:progress and data (the raw chunk JSON, NOT re-wrapped). A final event:end frame is emitted when the execution reaches a terminal state and the stream then closes; event:error is sent if the LISTEN connection drops. Keepalive :ping comments keep proxies from idling the connection; the terminal-close poll cadence is a modest default bounded by the configured SSE keepalive interval. AUTH: this route inherits the management API's configured auth middleware (HarvestPlugin::api_with_auth); it is deliberately NOT admin-gated (AC5 — end-users stream their own workflows). If no api_with_auth middleware is configured the route is open — embedders exposing streams to untrusted end-users should configure api_with_auth or front it with their own auth. The engine only checks that the execution exists (else 404) — exec_id is effectively a bearer capability for this run's live chunk CONTENT, so embedders exposing sensitive output MUST add per-execution authorization. Each subscriber holds one dedicated (non-pooled) Postgres LISTEN connection for the stream's lifetime; embedders should rate-limit and/or cap concurrent streams per user to avoid DB connection exhaustion (a global concurrent-stream cap is a possible future enhancement).

200.description: Content-Type: text/event-stream. Frames: event:progress (data = the published chunk JSON, id = monotonic seq), a terminal event:end, or event:error. If the execution is already terminal at connect, a single event:end frame is sent and the stream closes. SEQ CLIENT CONTRACT: id is a monotonic per-execution LOGICAL-POSITION identity (not a per-chunk counter). Subscribers should dedupe by seq (keep-first) for at-most-once-per-position display, and use forward seq JUMPS to detect gaps after reconnect. A re-driven workflow position re-emits the SAME seq (best-effort); a re-emitted chunk MAY carry different content for non-deterministic chunks — the first-delivered is canonical. seq is per exec_id; a continue-as-new successor is a new exec_id on a new stream whose seq restarts. Chunks may be DROPPED best-effort under back-pressure (slow client) — the monotonic seq lets the client detect the resulting gap.

get.description: Reconstruct a single execution's timeline (per-step durations, busy-vs-wait split, slowest step) purely from recorded history; no new events are appended and no state is recomputed. Classic DAG runs are not on the execution path and return 404; unified DAG runs lower onto the standard execution path and return 200 like any workflow execution. The wait_ms/exec_ms split is present ONLY for regular activity steps that recorded a claim/start timestamp; it is null for child_workflow, local_activity, external activities (issue #92 — these render as activity steps with no split), timer, signal_wait, side_effect, and for activities with no recorded start. total_ms is always present. Rollup attribution: a started activity's queue-wait split goes to rollup.wait_ms and its exec split to rollup.busy_ms; a regular activity (one reporting an attempt) with a null split never started (pending or a schedule-to-start timeout) so its whole total_ms is queue-wait and goes to rollup.wait_ms; external activities, child_workflow, local_activity, and side_effect totals go to rollup.busy_ms; timer and signal_wait totals go to rollup.wait_ms. For a retried activity, wait_ms spans all prior attempts' execution and backoff, not only queue wait — treat it as an upper bound on queue wait. Known limitation: the full event history is loaded with no LIMIT (bounded by workflow continue-as-new discipline, the ≤500-event target), so a run with a very large history makes this read proportionally expensive.

get.description: Recursive cross-shard execution lineage tree (issue #621): the full descendant tree rooted at {id}, so an operator triaging a DLQ/stuck alert can locate the failed descendant of a multi-level saga in ONE call instead of hand-walking parent_id links level by level and shard by shard. Rooting at a mid-tree node returns just the subtree below it; the chosen root is always depth 0 and still reports its own parent_id. Each node carries execution_id, workflow_name, workflow_id, state, started_at, closed_at, parent_id, depth, shard_id, and the spawn relationship (await_mode `awaited`/`detached` plus parent_close_policy when detached); children is always an array, empty for a leaf (never an error). The walk fans out across every readable shard (the iter_shards() aggregation pattern), so a child placed on a different shard than its parent by rendezvous hashing still appears. Recursion is bounded by max_depth (default 20, ceiling 50) and max_nodes (default 1000, ceiling 10000, counted INCLUDING the root); hitting either sets truncated=true with a machine-readable truncation_reason (`max_depth` | `max_nodes`) and names the dropped subtrees' parents in truncated_parent_ids (bounded, with truncated_parents_capped when it overflowed) — never a silent cap. Only parents that PROVABLY have children are named (via a bounded existence probe), so an operator is never sent chasing a subtree that does not exist. A visited-set guarantees each execution_id appears exactly once and a malformed parent_id loop terminates instead of recursing. `?summary=true` returns the per-state DESCENDANT roll-up (counts keyed by lowercased state, every known state always present even at 0; the root's own state is echoed on `root` and excluded from counts) plus total_descendants, for an at-a-glance health check without transferring the tree. Cross-shard degradation (issue #756): an unreachable shard is named in unavailable_shards with status `partial`/`unavailable` rather than failing the whole call — a triage read must not 500 during the incident it exists to diagnose. NOT admin-gated, matching GET /workflows/{id}/children (which already traverses depth cross-shard over the same rows). SNAPSHOT CONSISTENCY: shards are read independently, so a tree may be marginally time-skewed across shards; acceptable for triage. Adds no WorkflowEvent variant, no migration, appends no events, performs no writes. A malformed percent-encoded query-string byte sequence (an invalid UTF-8 byte, or an incomplete/non-hex `%` escape) is rejected with a 400 before any parameter is parsed, rather than silently substituting the Unicode replacement character and proceeding with a wrong-but-plausible value (issue #1151, sweeping the issue #774 `queue-coverage` fix to every other raw-pairs route).

Default (tree) mode returns root (a nested node whose `children` array recurses), node_count, and max_depth_reached. `?summary=true` returns root as a compact {execution_id, workflow_name, workflow_id, state} ref plus counts (map of lowercased state -> descendant count) and total_descendants, and omits node_count/children. Both shapes carry truncated, truncation_reason (omitted when null), truncated_parent_ids, truncated_parents_capped, limits (the bounds actually applied), status, and unavailable_shards. The fields list above is the UNION of both shapes. retained_summary_parent_ids (issue #752) names nodes in the returned tree that have at least one child DEMOTED INTO A RETENTION SUMMARY and therefore omitted from the tree along with everything beneath it; it is empty unless tiered summary retention is enabled. It is a THIRD, independent incompleteness signal: truncated=false AND status=complete together still do not mean every descendant is present -- check this list too. The omitted rows remain readable via GET /workflows/summaries.

conflict_policy.description: How to handle a collision with a currently-ACTIVE (RUNNING/PAUSED) prior run (issue #685). Orthogonal to reuse_policy (which governs terminal priors). One of: unspecified (default — each reuse policy's native active behavior, byte-for-byte identical to today), fail (409 AlreadyExists), use_existing (return the existing run, 200, no new WorkflowStarted), terminate_existing (cancel the active prior and start fresh, 201). Sending the field (even 'unspecified') surfaces a started_fresh boolean in the response (true = fresh run created, false = attached to the existing run); omitting it keeps the response byte-for-byte identical to today. terminate_existing requires admin authentication, because it can cancel a live prior; the other values (unspecified, fail, use_existing) do not — except that unspecified inherits the reuse policy's native behavior, so reuse_policy=terminate_if_running with an omitted/unspecified conflict_policy still requires admin. Not supported combined with a throttle/debounce/batch policy — the start is deferred and has no active prior to resolve at request time (400). An unknown value returns 400. A prior sealed MIGRATED/MIGRATING by a shard rebalance (issue #964) counts as ACTIVE -- the run is live, just on another shard -- and terminate_existing against one is REFUSED with a retryable 503 naming the live residence rather than replaced: the terminate could not reach the live copy from the prior's shard, and replacing would release the business key while the real run kept executing, producing two live runs for one workflow_id. Cancel or terminate the execution by id (which routes to its live residence), then retry the start.

idempotency_key.description: Request-scoped idempotency key (issue #808). Two starts carrying the same key within the retention window (default 24h) converge on exactly one execution: the first creates it, the second returns the same execution_id as a no-op (200, no second WorkflowStarted, no second task). Dedup scope is (workflow_name, idempotency_key), independent of workflow_id, and short-circuits the reuse_policy matrix. A committed keyed replay short-circuits to the 200 no-op before fresh-start-only validations (input-schema #373, completion-callback SSRF #605, delay/start_at) and before the admission gate #377, returning the original execution regardless of the retry's body; a genuinely fresh keyed start (no live claim) still runs every validation and the gate. The `Idempotency-Key` request header takes precedence over this body field; a present-but-empty key returns 400. Mutually exclusive with a throttle/debounce/batch policy (400 if combined). Shard routing: a keyed start with an OMITTED (auto-generated) workflow_id routes by the key so same-key retries co-locate and dedup; a keyed start with an EXPLICIT workflow_id routes by workflow_id (preserving the reuse_policy matrix and the shard-local (workflow_name, workflow_id) uniqueness invariant). For dedup to converge across a delivery's retries, be consistent about supplying vs. omitting workflow_id.

An undeclared or blank key returns 400 rather than falling back to the rendezvous hash.

Returns 400 when the shard is outside the deployment's readable_shards, has been drained out of writable_shards, is negative, or is the reserved routing sentinel — never a silent fallback to the default shard. The pinned shard is inherited by child workflows, continue-as-new successors, workflow-level retries, and reset forks, so residency is transitive across the whole workflow tree. Consistency caveat: for a given workflow_id, pin consistently across every start — an unpinned start of the same workflow_id routes by hash to a different shard and cannot see the pinned run, so the shard-local (workflow_name, workflow_id) uniqueness invariant would not catch it. A retry of a keyed start must likewise repeat the same placement, since the placement determines which shard holds the idempotency claim.

When the request sends a conflict_policy field (even 'unspecified'), the response includes started_fresh (true = created a new run, false = attached to the existing run); omitting conflict_policy omits started_fresh so the response is byte-for-byte identical to today. Returns 200 with {..., started_fresh: false, deduplicated: true} when an idempotency_key (issue #808) matched an earlier same-key start (no new execution created); a fresh idempotency_key start returns 201 with {..., started_fresh: true, deduplicated: false}. post.description: Atomically start a workflow if no live run for (workflow_name, workflow_id) exists, or attach to the existing run otherwise, and admit exactly one update in the same shard-local transaction (issue #479). Mirrors the reuse-policy matrix of signal-with-start but for request/response updates. PAUSED executions are rejected 409. A validator attached to the update handler runs inside the transaction; rejection rolls back any fresh WorkflowStarted event.

parameters.description: Registered workflow function name.
parameters.name: workflow_name

execution_timeout_secs.description: Overall execution timeout in seconds, applied only on fresh start.

id_reuse_policy.description: Duplicate-id policy: allow_duplicate (default), reject_duplicate, allow_duplicate_failed_only, or terminate_if_running.

idempotency_key.description: Optional dedup key. Derives update_id via UUIDv5 so retries with the same key return the cached outcome without re-admitting.

memo.description: Non-indexed metadata (JSON object) used only when a fresh execution is started.

queue.description: Task queue name used only when a fresh execution is started.

search_attrs.description: Indexed search attributes (JSON object) used only when a fresh execution is started.

start_input.description: Workflow input payload applied only when a fresh execution is started.

timeout_secs.description: Maximum seconds to poll when wait_for_stage=completed. Defaults to 30.

update_args.description: Update arguments (any JSON value). Defaults to null.

update_name.description: Registered update handler name to invoke on the execution.

wait_for_stage.description: Whether to poll for update completion. 'completed' (default) polls until the update handler finishes and returns the result; 'admitted' returns immediately after the update is admitted to history.

workflow_id.description: Stable identifier used to deduplicate concurrent starts.

200.description: An existing live execution was attached instead of a fresh one being started.

201.description: Returns 200 when an existing live execution is attached rather than a fresh one started.

400.description: Invalid request body, workflow name, id_reuse_policy, or update validator rejection.

409.description: Duplicate workflow_id with id_reuse_policy=reject_duplicate, or execution is PAUSED.

429.description: The workflow's declared per-tenant resource quota (issue #946, QuotaPolicy) is exhausted for the resolved key on a FRESH admission only (attaching to an existing run and admitting the update against it never re-checks the quota). Body is {"error": "quota exceeded", "workflow_name", "key", "resource", "limit", "current"}, mirroring the plain start route's arm exactly. Never returned for a workflow with no declared QuotaPolicy.

gate_id.description: The gate that blocked the start.

reason.description: The gate's stated reason.

503.description: An admission gate blocked the start. Retry once the gate clears.

504.description: The update did not complete within the wait window. The execution was started and the update was admitted; poll the update result.
